big_idea: Every multiplication fact up to 10×10 can be shown as an array.
learning_intention: We are learning to represent any multiplication fact up to 10×10 as an array and find the related division facts.
student_learning_goal: I can represent any multiplication fact up to 10×10 as an array and find the related division.
success_criteria: I can build any multiplication up to 10×10 as an array of dots.
I can use a known fact (like 5×7=35) to solve a related fact (6×7).
I can write the division for any multiplication up to 100÷10.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Maya the Multiplication Maven — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Anchor chart 'Use What You Know' with example breakdown (6×7 = 5×7 + 1×7)
Per-pair set of array grid + counters
Lesson 3 array tracker — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: Maya knows 5×7=35. How can she figure out 6×7? Maya opens: 'Big fact STUCK? Use a near fact!' Pixel cheers: 'Big facts? PRACTICE the near fact!'
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Maya puppet in hand. 'Friends — yesterday we mastered the 2s, 5s, 10s. Today we tackle ALL the multiplications up to 10×10. Even the tricky ones.'

'Maya knows 5×7=35. But she doesn't remember 6×7. What can she do?'

Take responses. Some children say 'count up by 7'. Some say 'add 7 to 35'. Affirm.

Build 5×7 array on the grid (5 rows × 7 columns of counters = 35). 'Maya knows this is 35. Now she adds ONE MORE ROW of 7.' Add the 6th row. Count: 35 + 7 = 42. So 6 × 7 = 42.

Write the rule: 6 × 7 = 5 × 7 + 1 × 7 = 35 + 7 = 42. 'This is the DISTRIBUTIVE PROPERTY. Break a hard fact into easy facts.'

Practice: 7 × 8. 'Hmm — what do you know nearby?' Children: '5 × 8 = 40' (because of yesterday). 'And 7 × 8 = 5 × 8 + 2 × 8 = 40 + 16 = 56.' Build the array.

Now division. '56 ÷ 8 = ?' '7' (from the fact family). '56 ÷ 7 = ?' '8'. 'Multiplication and division go TOGETHER.'

'Today we'll build arrays for tricky facts AND practice the divisions.'
student_actions: Watch Maya extend a 5×7 array to a 6×7 array.
Help apply the distributive property to find 7×8.

steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Use what you know to solve what you don't.' Walk through each, showing both build-and-extend AND break-down strategies.

steps.instruction: Send pairs to three stations (~7 min each). Station A: Array Build for Tricky Facts — 8 cards with facts like 6×7, 8×9, 7×6; pair builds the array, writes the multiplication AND the related division. Station B: Multiplication Chart — pair fills in the 1-10 chart (10×10 grid), discussing patterns. Station C: Use What You Know — 8 cards each with a tricky fact + a hint (5×7=35); pair uses the hint to derive the answer.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Three stations, 7 minutes each.'

steps.instruction: Stretch challenge at Station C: include 4 facts WITHOUT hints. Children must derive what hint to use. (For 8×9: use 8×10-8 or 5×9+3×9.)
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to pairs: 'For these, decide WHICH known fact will help. Write the breakdown.'

steps.instruction: Discuss patterns in the multiplication chart. (a) The diagonal contains squares: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100. (b) The chart is symmetric across the diagonal (4×6 = 6×4). (c) Multiples of 5 always end in 0 or 5; multiples of 10 always end in 0.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Look at the chart. What patterns do you see?' Lead to: diagonal, symmetry, ones-digit patterns.

steps.instruction: Circulate to record formative evidence on the array tracker.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Ask 'Show me 7×6 with an array. What's the related division?' Mark the tracker.

steps.instruction: STRATEGY COMPARE: Two pairs share their derivation paths for 6×7 — Pair A '6×5 + 6×2'; Pair B '6×10 - 6×3'. Class compares which is faster. Cite Baroody (2006) derived-fact strategies.
steps.teacher_prompt: Maya: 'Different anchors, same fact. Pick the anchor your brain trusts.'

differentiation.for_emerging: Stay at Station A. Build only ×3 and ×4 facts to extend from yesterday's ×2 fluency.
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch to facts in the 11-12 range (11×7, 12×6). Discuss whether the chart pattern extends.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide picture-supported fact cards. Pair with strong-recall peer for Station C.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Skip-count by 6s, 7s, 8s, 9s as a class — body movement reinforces the multiplication-as-skip-count link.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: builds an array for any fact up to 10×10; uses distributive property to derive a tricky fact; writes the related division correctly.
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the array tracker per child.
tracker_columns: Builds array for any fact up to 10×10

discussion_prompts: What's the distributive property? Show with an example.
If you know 5×7=35, how does that help with 6×7?
Where do you see PATTERNS in the multiplication chart?
consolidation.exit_routine: Maya's derived-fact chant — 'Big fact STUCK? Use a near fact!' Class echoes. (3x). Each child writes one derived fact with the anchor named. Pixel's send-off: 'Derive, practice, REPEAT!'

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Array building for any fact up to 10×10, distributive property application, related division accuracy.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 3 captures B2.6 mastery. Children at L4 fluently use the distributive property for any tricky fact and write all 4 facts of the family.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child knows 5×3 but freezes on 7×8 — repairing the derived-fact gap
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On 10×10 multiplication, the trap is derived-fact missing: child has memorised some facts but cannot DERIVE harder ones from known. Baroody (2006) on derived-fact strategies and Anghileri (2001) on multiplication learning frame this. Without derivation strategies, 7×8 stays stuck.

Yesterday Maya introduced 2s/5s/10s. Today: derive the rest (7×8 = 7×10 - 7×2 = 56). Lesson 4 numerator; Lesson 5 ratios.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station A. The card says 7×8. The child stares blankly. 'I don't know it.'
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch beside the child. 'You don't know 7×8 directly — but you DO know other facts. Let's use them.'

'What's 5×8?' '40' (from Lesson 2). 'Right. And what's 2×8?' '16'. 'So 5×8 + 2×8 = 40 + 16 = 56.' Show the array: 5 rows × 8 columns + 2 rows × 8 columns. 'That's 7×8.'

'OR — what's 10×8?' '80'. 'And what's 7 less than 10? 3. So 10×8 - 3×8 = 80 - 24 = 56.'

Two paths, same answer.

Now the rule. 'Maya says — break the hard fact into easy facts. Use what you know.'

Have the child derive 9×6. Wait. 'I know 10×6 = 60. So 9×6 = 60 - 1×6 = 54.' Affirm.

If the child STILL stalls on subsequent facts: build with arrays for every fact for the next 5 minutes. The visual evidence reinforces the breakdown.

Long-term recovery: daily warm-up with a 'derive this fact' challenge. 5 facts per day. The reflex builds within 2 weeks.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Stalls or guesses on facts outside ×2/×5/×10. Most common at start of Lesson 3.
(Mid) Derives with prompts; doesn't yet auto-break the fact.
(Stretched) Volunteers multiple breakdowns: '7×8 = 5×8+2×8 = 40+16 = 56, OR 8×8-8 = 64-8 = 56.' Sees alternatives.
common_misconceptions: Multiplication facts are all separate things to memorise. (Repair: distributive property breaks them into smaller pieces.)
Bigger × harder. (Children avoid 8×9 thinking it's harder than 4×9. Repair: 8×9 can be 4×9 doubled — same difficulty.)
If I don't know it, I can't get it. (Repair: arrays make any fact derivable from smaller pieces.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child blanks on 7×8: drill 'use a NEAR fact — 7×10 = 70, minus 7×2 = 14, so 7×8 = 56'; chunk strategy.
DIAGNOSTIC B — child can derive but won't articulate: force the sentence frame 'I used ___ × ___ as my anchor; then I ___'.
DIAGNOSTIC C — child confuses multiplication with division: drill the inverse — '7×8 = 56, so 56÷7 = 8'; physical array demo.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of B2.6 (multiplication to 10×10 via arrays and distributive property).
